• **Performance Grading Index (PGI):** The **Performance Grading Index (PGI)** is a comprehensive tool designed to assess the performance of states and union territories in terms of school education.
 
• The PGI evaluates states and UTs based on various parameters such as **access, equity, infrastructure, governance, and learning outcomes**.
 
• **Ministry of Education:** The **Ministry of Education**, Government of India, releases the PGI every year to provide insights into the quality of school education across states and UTs. *Hence, the correct answer is the Ministry of Education.*

• **Objective of PGI:**

 
 
• The PGI aims to create an objective mechanism to provide states and UTs with feedback on their performance in school education.
 
• It serves as a tool for improving the education system by identifying weaknesses in critical areas such as **equity, governance, and learning outcomes**.
 
 
 
• **Parameters assessed in PGI:**
 
 
• The PGI evaluates states based on **70 indicators**, including categories like **infrastructure, teacher training, and student achievements**.
 
• The indicators are divided into five broad categories: **access, equity, infrastructure & facilities, governance processes, and learning outcomes.**
 
• For instance, states like Kerala and Tamil Nadu often perform well due to their robust education systems and governance mechanisms.
 
 
 
• **Importance of PGI:**
 
 
• The PGI provides a comparative analysis of states, encouraging healthy competition and improvement in school education quality.
 
• It helps policymakers identify areas requiring immediate attention and guides them in allocating resources effectively.
 
• The PGI aligns with the objectives of the **National Education Policy (NEP) 2020**, which aims to provide equitable and inclusive education to all students.

• The PGI framework was developed by the **Ministry of Education** and is widely regarded as a revolutionary step towards improving education quality in India.
 
• It emphasizes the importance of governance and equity in improving educational outcomes.
 
 
 
• **States’ Performance:**
 
 
• States such as **Kerala, Punjab, and Chandigarh** have consistently performed well in PGI due to their focus on education quality and robust infrastructure.
 
• On the other hand, states with weaker education systems, such as **Bihar and Jharkhand**, have shown gradual improvement due to targeted interventions.
 
• The PGI encourages states to adopt best practices from top-performing states and improve their education systems.

questions.question: According to the Census of India data, what was the overall population density of India in 2011?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**382 person/km²**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **population density** is defined as the number of people living per unit area, typically calculated as persons per square kilometer (**person/km²**).
 
• According to the **2011 Census of India**, the overall population density of India was recorded at **382 person/km²**. This is calculated by dividing the total population by the total land area of the country.
 
• The total population of India in **2011** was approximately **1.21 billion**, while the total geographical area of India is around **3.28 million square kilometers**.
 
• The figure of **382 person/km²** represents a significant increase compared to the population density of **325 person/km²** recorded in the **2001 Census**. This reflects the rapid population growth in India over the decade.
 
• *Hence, option 1 (382 person/km²) is correct.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] Additional Information__

__
 
• **Population Density Across States:**

 
 
• The **state of Bihar** had the highest population density in 2011, with **1,106 person/km²**, reflecting its high population concentration.
 
• In contrast, **Arunachal Pradesh** recorded the lowest population density, with only **17 person/km²**, due to its vast geographical area and sparse population.
 
 
 
• **Global Comparison:**
 
 
• India's population density of **382 person/km²** in 2011 is significantly higher than the global average, which was approximately **50 person/km²** around the same time.
 
• Countries like **Bangladesh** and **Japan** also have high population densities, with figures exceeding **1,000 person/km²** in urban regions.
 
 
 
• **Factors Influencing Population Density:**
 
 
• **Geography:** Fertile plains such as the Indo-Gangetic plain have higher population densities due to their suitability for agriculture.
 
• **Urbanization:** Cities like **Delhi**, **Mumbai**, and **Kolkata** have extremely high densities due to economic opportunities and infrastructure development.
 
• **Climate:** Harsh climatic conditions in areas like the Thar Desert or Himalayan regions result in lower population densities.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Census of India:**

 
 
• Conducted every **10 years**, the Census of India provides critical data on population, demographics, and socio-economic conditions.
 
• The **2011 Census** was the 15th National Census since 1872 and is considered one of the largest administrative exercises globally.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Population Density Data:**
 
 
• Used by policymakers to allocate resources, plan urban development, and implement welfare schemes.
 
• Helps in identifying areas needing focused development, such as rural regions with low densities or overcrowded cities.

questions.question: By what name is the substance that slows down the rate of a chemical reaction known?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**inhibitor**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• Inhibitors can be classified into several types based on their mechanism, such as **competitive inhibitors**, which compete with reactants for active sites, or **non-competitive inhibitors**, which bind to different parts of the molecule.
 
• An inhibitor does not necessarily stop the reaction altogether but significantly slows down its **rate**. This property makes it distinct from catalysts, which increase the reaction rate.
 
• In industrial applications, inhibitors are used to control undesirable side reactions or to ensure safety during chemical processes. *Hence, the correct answer is inhibitor.*

**Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Characteristics of Inhibitors:**

 
 
• **Types:** Includes competitive inhibitors, non-competitive inhibitors, uncompetitive inhibitors, and mixed inhibitors.
 
• **Catalysts:** Increase the rate of a chemical reaction without being consumed.
 
• **Corrosion inhibitors:** Substances used to slow down the corrosion of metals.
 
• **Polymerization inhibitors:** Added to monomers to prevent unwanted polymerization during storage or transportation.
 
 

**Important Points__**

 
• **Applications of Inhibitors:**

 
 
• **Medicinal Uses:** Enzyme inhibitors are widely used in pharmaceuticals to treat diseases such as hypertension, cancer, and viral infections.
 
 
 
• **Environmental Impact:**
 
 
• Biodegradable inhibitors are being developed to reduce environmental harm while maintaining effectiveness.

__
 
• **Akbarnama:** Written by **Abul Fazl**, Akbarnama is a historic document chronicling the reign of Mughal Emperor Akbar. It is divided into three sections or volumes. 
 
• The **third section** of Akbarnama, also known as **Ain-i-Akbari**, extensively describes Akbar’s administration, including his household, army, revenue system, and the geography of his empire. 
 
• The **Ain-i-Akbari** contains detailed information about Akbar's centralized administration, military organization, and governance strategies. 
 
• The **first section** focuses on the genealogy and history of Akbar’s ancestors, providing a historical background of the Mughal dynasty. It does not include administrative details. Hence, this statement is **incorrect**.
 
• The **second section** narrates Akbar’s reign, detailing his conquests and campaigns but does not delve into administrative topics. Hence, this statement is **incorrect**.
 
• **Therefore, the third section is the only part of Akbarnama that discusses Akbar’s administration, household, army, revenue, and geography.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Structure of Akbarnama:**

 
 
• The **First Section**: It narrates the genealogy of Akbar, describing his ancestors and their achievements, and provides a historical backdrop to the Mughal Empire.
 
• The **Second Section**: Focuses on significant events during Akbar’s reign, such as conquests, campaigns, and efforts to expand the empire.
 
• The **Third Section (Ain-i-Akbari)**: Extensively details Akbar’s administrative framework, revenue policies, military organization, and socio-economic conditions of the empire.
 
 
 
• **Features of Ain-i-Akbari:**
 
 
• Describes Akbar’s administrative divisions, including provinces (**subahs**), districts, and villages.
 
• Details Akbar’s **revenue system**, including land measurement, taxation policies, and agricultural land categorization.
 
• Explains the **Mansabdari system**, military hierarchy, and recruitment policies.
 
• Provides insights into the socio-cultural environment, royal household operations, and religious practices during Akbar’s reign.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Akbarnama:**
 
 
• **Akbarnama** serves as a crucial historical source for understanding the Mughal Empire’s governance, military strategies, and socio-economic conditions.
 
• Reflects Akbar’s **visionary leadership** and policies of religious tolerance and cultural integration.
 
• Highlights Akbar’s emphasis on a **centralized administration** and efforts to enhance the welfare of his subjects.
 
 
 
• **About Abul Fazl:**
 
 
• Abul Fazl, a **court historian**, was one of the **Navaratnas (Nine Jewels)** in Akbar’s court. 
 
• He played a significant role in shaping Akbar’s governance policies and documenting his reign through the Akbarnama.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Chronology and Historical Context:**

 
 
• The Akbarnama was written during Akbar's reign, emphasizing the importance of documenting history contemporaneously.
 
• It provides insights into how historical records were meticulously maintained in the Mughal era.
 
 
 
• **Relevance in Modern Times:**
 
 
• The Akbarnama is frequently referenced in academic studies related to medieval Indian history.
 
• It serves as an inspiration for modern governance and administration due to its detailed description of Akbar’s visionary policies.

questions.question: What is a key indicator of economic growth that has shown sustained improvement in India since 1991?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**foreign exchange reserves**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** 

__
 
• **Foreign exchange reserves** are crucial economic indicators that reflect the financial stability and economic growth of a country.
 
• Since the **economic liberalization** reforms introduced in **1991**, India has seen a substantial increase in its foreign exchange reserves due to improved economic policies and trade liberalization.
 
• Foreign exchange reserves consist of assets like **foreign currencies, gold reserves, and Special Drawing Rights (SDRs)** maintained by the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)**.
 
• The significant rise in reserves since **1991** is attributed to increased foreign investment, export growth, and remittance inflows. These reserves play a pivotal role in stabilizing the Indian economy against external shocks.
 
• India’s foreign exchange reserves reached over **USD 600 billion** in **2021**, making it one of the highest among emerging economies.
 
• **Functions:** Foreign exchange reserves are used to manage currency fluctuations, stabilize the **rupee**, and meet external debt obligations.
 
• They also act as a buffer during economic crises, enabling the government to maintain liquidity in the foreign exchange market. *Hence, foreign exchange reserves are a key indicator of sustained economic improvement in India.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Fiscal deficit:**

 
 
• **Fiscal deficit** refers to the shortfall between the government’s revenue and expenditure. While it is an important economic measure, it does not directly indicate sustained economic growth.
 
• A high fiscal deficit can lead to inflationary pressures, whereas a controlled deficit indicates financial discipline. India’s fiscal deficit has been a challenge but is not the primary indicator of sustained growth since 1991.
 
 
 
• **Black money:**
 
 
• Black money refers to unaccounted or illicit wealth that is not taxed or reported. While efforts have been made to curb black money, its presence negatively impacts the economy and cannot be considered an indicator of growth.
 
• The government has implemented measures such as demonetization (2016) and stricter compliance to address black money, but it is not directly linked to sustained economic improvement.
 
 
 
• **Infant mortality rate:**
 
 
• The **infant mortality rate** measures the number of deaths of infants under one year per 1,000 live births. It is an indicator of healthcare quality and social development, but it does not directly reflect economic growth.
 
• India has made significant progress in reducing infant mortality rates through healthcare initiatives, but this is not the key indicator of sustained economic improvement.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key Features of Foreign Exchange Reserves:**

 
 
• India’s foreign exchange reserves include **foreign currencies, gold, SDRs, and reserve positions in the IMF**. They are managed by the **Reserve Bank of India**.
 
• 
 
• 
• These reserves are crucial for maintaining economic stability, supporting imports, and ensuring the country’s ability to repay external debts.
 
 
 
• **Global Comparison:**
 
 
• India ranks among the top countries globally in terms of foreign exchange reserves, alongside **China, Japan, and Switzerland**.
 
• **China** has the largest reserves globally, exceeding **USD 3 trillion**, while India’s reserves have steadily grown since 1991.

questions.question: Which of the following is the Directive Principle of State Policy mentioned under Article 48A of the Indian Constitution?

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 48A** of the **Indian Constitution** is a part of the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP), which enjoins the state to protect and improve the environment and safeguard the forests and wildlife of the country.
 
• This article was inserted into the Constitution by the **42nd Amendment Act, 1976**, which emphasized environmental protection as a fundamental directive for the state.
 
• The provision underlines the responsibility of the state to ensure a healthy environment, including the improvement of ecosystems and natural habitats. *Hence, statement 4 is correct.*
 
• Article 48A aligns with the broad objectives of sustainable development and recognizes the critical importance of environmental conservation for future generations.
 
• The inclusion of this article underscores India's commitment to global environmental concerns and its intent to integrate sustainable development into policymaking.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP):**

 
 
• The DPSPs are non-justiciable provisions listed in **Part IV of the Indian Constitution**. These principles are fundamental in the governance of the country and aim to achieve socio-economic justice.
 
• While not enforceable in a court of law, they act as guidelines for the state to implement policies and laws that promote the welfare of the people.
 
 
 
• **42nd Amendment Act, 1976:**
 
 
• The 42nd Amendment Act is also known as the "**Mini Constitution**" due to the wide range of changes it brought to the Indian Constitution.
 
• It added **Article 48A** under the DPSP and **Article 51A(g)** under Fundamental Duties, making environmental protection a responsibility of both the state and citizens.
 
 
 
• **Key Features of Article 48A:**
 
 
• **Focus:** Aimed at the protection and improvement of the **environment**, including forests and wildlife.
 
• **Importance:** It establishes the foundation for the enactment of environmental laws and regulations in India, like the **Environment Protection Act, 1986**.
 
• **Global Relevance:** Aligns with global environmental principles and India's commitment to international conventions on environmental protection.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Other Relevant DPSPs:**

 
 
• **Article 40:** Relates to the organization of **Gram Panchayats**, encouraging decentralized governance. *This is not related to Article 48A and is incorrect.*
 
• **Article 47:** Directs the state to raise the level of **nutrition** and improve public health. *This is not associated with environmental protection and is incorrect.*
 
• **Article 39A:** Provides for **legal aid** to weaker sections to promote justice on equal footing. *This is unrelated to environmental protection and is incorrect.*
 
 
 
• **Environmental Laws in India:**
 
 
• **Environment Protection Act, 1986:** Enacted to implement decisions of the United Nations Conference on the Human Environment held in 1972.
 
• **Wildlife Protection Act, 1972:** Aimed at protecting wildlife and their habitats.
 
• **Forest Conservation Act, 1980:** Focused on restricting deforestation and promoting forest conservation.

questions.question: Which sector dominated India's national income before independence?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Agriculture**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Before India's independence, agriculture was the predominant sector** contributing to the national income. The Indian economy was primarily agrarian in nature, with a majority of the population engaged in farming and related activities.
 
• The **British colonial policies** led to the exploitation of Indian agriculture, which was mainly subsistence-based. Despite this, agriculture remained the backbone of the economy, contributing to over **50% of the national income**.
 
• Industries and services such as trade, transport, and banking were underdeveloped and contributed only a small fraction to the national income. *Hence, agriculture was the dominant sector in the economy.*
 
• The majority of the population, approximately **70-80%, depended on agriculture** for their livelihood. This dependence on agriculture was due to the lack of industrialization and minimal focus on other economic sectors.
 
• The agricultural sector faced significant issues such as **low productivity, outdated techniques, and excessive taxation**. Despite these challenges, it remained the primary source of income and employment. *Hence, agriculture was the dominant sector before independence.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Agriculture in Pre-Independence India:**

 
 
• **Agriculture was the largest contributor** to the economy, but it was heavily exploited under British rule. The **Permanent Settlement Act of 1793** introduced the zamindari system, which burdened farmers with heavy taxes.
 
• The focus of British policies was on maximizing revenue rather than improving agricultural productivity. This resulted in periodic famines and economic distress for farmers.
 
• The introduction of **cash crops** such as cotton, indigo, and opium for export further impacted food grain production. This shift prioritized British economic interests over local needs.
 
 
 
• **Other Economic Sectors before Independence:**
 
 
• **Industry:** The industrial sector was underdeveloped and consisted mainly of small-scale industries such as textiles and handicrafts. The **deindustrialization** caused by British policies led to the decline of traditional industries.
 
• **Trade and Transport:** Trade was primarily focused on exporting raw materials to Britain and importing finished goods. The development of railways was aimed at facilitating this trade rather than fostering domestic growth.
 
• **Banking:** The banking sector was limited and served primarily British economic interests. Indian-owned banks were few and had a minimal role in the economy.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key Features of Agriculture Before Independence:**

 
 
• The agricultural sector was characterized by **subsistence farming**, with farmers using traditional methods and tools.
 
• The **Green Revolution** and advancements in agriculture took place much later, post-independence, to improve productivity and reduce dependency on imports.
 
• The exploitation of farmers through **heavy land taxes**, low remuneration for crops, and lack of irrigation facilities were major issues.
 
 
 
• **Contribution of Other Sectors:**
 
 
• The **industrial sector** contributed minimally to the economy due to the lack of investment and infrastructure.
 
• The **services sector**, including banking and transport, remained underdeveloped and served colonial interests rather than the local economy.

questions.question: Which of the following laws provides reservation in education and employment to the Economically Weaker Sections (EWS)?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**103rd Constitutional Amendment**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **103rd Constitutional Amendment Act**, enacted in **2019**, introduced reservation for the **Economically Weaker Sections (EWS)** of society in education and employment.
 
• This amendment added **Article 15(6)** and **Article 16(6)** to the Constitution of India, enabling the government to provide up to **10% reservation** for EWS in higher education and government jobs.
 
• The criteria for EWS reservation are based on **economic indicators**, such as annual family income and land ownership, and exclude individuals from the **Scheduled Castes (SC), Scheduled Tribes (ST), and Other Backward Classes (OBC)**. *Hence, this amendment specifically caters to economically weaker individuals among the unreserved categories.*
 
• The amendment was a significant step towards addressing economic inequality and providing opportunities to disadvantaged sections of society who were previously excluded from affirmative action.
 
• The reservation under the **103rd Amendment** is **horizontal** in nature and does not overlap with existing reservations for other categories. *Hence, this amendment is directly linked to the question.*
 
• The amendment has been upheld by the **Supreme Court of India** as constitutionally valid after challenges were raised questioning its legality.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **103rd Constitutional Amendment Act:**

 
 
• This amendment was passed by the **Indian Parliament** in January **2019** and came into effect immediately.
 
• It provides up to **10% reservation** for **Economically Weaker Sections (EWS)** in admission to educational institutions (except minority institutions) and government jobs.
 
• The key eligibility criteria for EWS reservation include an annual family income of less than **₹8 lakh**, land ownership limits, and property ownership limits.
 
 
 
• **Other Constitutional Amendments:**
 
 
• **100th Constitutional Amendment:** This amendment ratified the **India-Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement** in **2015**, facilitating the exchange of enclaves between the two countries.
 
• **102nd Constitutional Amendment:** Enacted in **2018**, it granted constitutional status to the **National Commission for Backward Classes (NCBC)** and included provisions for identifying OBCs.
 
• **104th Constitutional Amendment:** Passed in **2020**, it extended reservations for **Scheduled Castes (SC)** and **Scheduled Tribes (ST)** in Lok Sabha and State Assemblies for another 10 years but removed reservation for Anglo-Indian representation.
 
 
 
• **Impact of EWS Reservation:**
 
 
• The EWS reservation aims to address economic disparities and ensure equal opportunities for economically disadvantaged individuals from the general category.
 
• It has led to increased access to education and employment for the EWS population, bridging gaps in socioeconomic development.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Eligibility Criteria for EWS Reservation:**

 
 
• Annual family income must be less than **₹8 lakh**.
 
• The family should not own agricultural land exceeding **5 acres** or residential plots exceeding specific area limits (1000 sq. ft. for urban areas).
 
 
 
• **Judicial Validation:**
 
 
• The **Supreme Court** upheld the constitutional validity of the **103rd Amendment**, stating that it does not violate the principle of equality.
 
• The judgment emphasized the need for affirmative action to support economically weaker sections.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Other Reservations:**
 
 
• EWS reservation is purely based on **economic criteria**, unlike SC/ST and OBC reservations, which are based on social and educational backwardness.

questions.question: Which blood vessels carry oxygenated blood from the heart to all parts of the body in humans?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Artery**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Arteries** are the blood vessels that carry **oxygenated blood** away from the heart to all parts of the body.
 
• The **pulmonary arteries** are an exception as they carry **deoxygenated blood** from the heart to the lungs.
 
• The oxygen-rich blood is pumped by the heart's left ventricle into the **aorta**, the largest artery, which branches out into smaller arteries and delivers oxygen to tissues.
 
• Arteries have **thick, elastic walls** to withstand the high pressure of blood being pumped by the heart.
 
• They play a crucial role in maintaining the **circulatory system** and ensuring that all body tissues receive oxygen and nutrients for proper functioning.
 
• Arteries also help regulate blood pressure through the elasticity of their walls, which can expand and contract based on the body's requirements.
 
• Veins, venules, and capillaries serve different purposes and do not carry oxygenated blood from the heart to the body tissues. Hence, the correct answer is Artery.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Veins:**

 
 
• Veins carry **deoxygenated blood** back to the heart, except for the pulmonary veins, which carry oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart.
 
• They have **thin walls** and are equipped with **valves** to prevent backflow of blood.
 
 
 
• **Venules:**
 
 
• Venules are small blood vessels that collect blood from capillaries and transport it to veins.
 
• They play a role in connecting the capillaries to the larger veins.
 
 
 
• **Capillaries:**
 
 
• Capillaries are the **smallest blood vessels** where the exchange of oxygen, carbon dioxide, nutrients, and waste products occurs between blood and tissues.
 
• They connect arteries and veins and have **thin walls** to facilitate diffusion of substances.
 
 
 
• **Function of Arteries:**
 
 
• Arteries ensure the supply of oxygenated blood to vital organs, maintaining their proper functioning.
 
• Examples include the **coronary arteries** (supplying the heart), **renal arteries** (supplying the kidneys), and **carotid arteries** (supplying the brain).

questions.question: Which of the following can have high optical density but low mass density?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Turpentine**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Optical density** refers to the ability of a material to slow down the speed of light passing through it. Materials with high refractive indices tend to have high optical density.
 
• On the other hand, **mass density** is the amount of mass per unit volume of a material. It is unrelated to optical density and is purely based on the physical composition of the material.
 
• **Turpentine**, a common organic solvent, has relatively high optical density due to its refractive index but low mass density compared to other materials like glass or germanium. *Hence, Turpentine satisfies the conditions mentioned in the question.*
 
• **Water** has lower optical density compared to turpentine or glass. While water has a moderate mass density, it does not exhibit high optical density. *Hence, water is not the correct answer.*
 
• **Germanium** is a dense material with both high optical density and high mass density. It does not meet the criteria for low mass density. *Hence, germanium is not the correct answer.*
 
• **Glass** has high optical density due to its refractive index but also possesses a higher mass density than turpentine. Thus, it does not meet the requirement for low mass density. *Hence, glass is not the correct answer.*
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Turpentine.***

**Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Key Characteristics of Turpentine:**

 
 
• **Composition:** Turpentine is an organic solvent derived from the resin of pine trees. It mainly contains terpenes.
 
• **Refractive Index:** Turpentine has a refractive index higher than water, which contributes to its high optical density.
 
• **Applications:** It is widely used in the **paint industry** as a solvent and thinner. Additionally, it is used in medical formulations and cleaning agents.
 
• **Mass Density:** Turpentine has a relatively low mass density, which makes it lighter compared to other materials like glass or germanium.
 
 
 
• **Key Characteristics of Other Options:**
 
 
• **Water:** Water has a refractive index of approximately 1.33, which is lower than that of turpentine or glass. Its mass density is 1 g/cm³.
 
• **Germanium:** A semiconductor material with high refractive index and high mass density. It is used in optical devices and electronics.
 
• **Glass:** Glass has a high refractive index but also has high mass density. It is commonly used in lenses, optical fibers, and construction.
 
 

**Important Points__**

 
• **Optical Density:**

 
 
• Materials with high optical density slow down light more effectively, causing phenomena like refraction.
 
• It is determined by the refractive index of the material.
 
 
 
• **Mass Density:**
 
 
• Mass density is measured in units like g/cm³ or kg/m³ and depends on the material's physical properties.
 
• Low mass density materials are typically lighter and less compact.

• The Mediterranean vegetation exhibits a significant level of **adaptation** to its environment, with plants often displaying deep root systems to access water from deeper soil layers.
 
• The region’s vegetation is not only ecologically significant but also economically important, with crops like **olives, grapes, and citrus fruits** being integral to agriculture and trade.
 
• Unlike mangroves, which grow in coastal saline water, or coniferous and deciduous forests, which thrive in colder or temperate climates, Mediterranean vegetation is uniquely suited to its hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters.

• **Aleppo pine:** A hardy species often found in hilly areas of the Mediterranean, adapted to arid climates.

questions.question: Which constitutional amendment gave constitutional status to the Panchayati Raj system in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992** provided **constitutional status to the Panchayati Raj system** in India, ensuring its establishment as a decentralized self-government in rural areas.
 
• This amendment added **Part IX** to the Indian Constitution, titled "**The Panchayats**," and incorporated **Articles 243 to 243-O**, laying down the framework for the Panchayati Raj system.
 
• The 73rd Amendment also introduced the **11th Schedule**, which contains a list of **29 functional items** that the Panchayats are responsible for, such as agriculture, rural housing, drinking water, roads, and education.
 
• This amendment made it **mandatory for states** to establish Panchayati Raj institutions in rural areas and conduct regular elections every **5 years**.
 
• The act provided for the establishment of a **three-tier structure** of Panchayati Raj, consisting of: **Gram Panchayat** (at the village level), **Panchayat Samiti** (at the block level), and **Zilla Parishad** (at the district level).
 
• It also introduced the concept of **reservation of seats** for Scheduled Castes (SCs), Scheduled Tribes (STs), and women in Panchayati Raj institutions to ensure inclusive participation in local governance.
 
• The State Election Commission was constituted to oversee the **free and fair elections** of Panchayati Raj institutions.
 
• The amendment empowered the state legislatures to endow Panchayats with **functional responsibilities** and authority for the preparation of plans for economic development and social justice.
 
• ***Hence, the 73rd Amendment Act of 1992 is the correct answer.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976:**

 
 
• This amendment is known as the "**Mini-Constitution**" as it brought about the most comprehensive changes to the Constitution.
 
• It introduced the **Fundamental Duties** under Part IVA (Article 51A).
 
• The amendment transferred several subjects from the **State List** to the **Concurrent List**, such as education, forests, and wildlife protection.
 
 
 
• **97th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011:**
 
 
• This amendment was related to **cooperative societies**. It gave constitutional status to cooperatives by adding **Part IXB** to the Constitution.
 
• It also included the **right to form cooperative societies** as a part of the Fundamental Rights under Article 19(1)(c).
 
 
 
• **74th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992:**
 
 
• This amendment provided a **constitutional status** to **urban local bodies**, such as Municipal Corporations, Municipal Councils, and Nagar Panchayats.
 
• It added **Part IXA** to the Constitution and introduced the **12th Schedule**, listing 18 functional items for urban local bodies.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key Features of Panchayati Raj System:**

 
 
• The system ensures **grassroots democracy** by empowering rural citizens to participate in governance.
 
• Panchayats are responsible for addressing **local issues**, such as water supply, sanitation, and rural development.
 
• The reservation system in Panchayati Raj promotes **social inclusion** and equitable representation in decision-making.
 
 
 
• **Impact of the 73rd Amendment:**
 
 
• The amendment strengthened **decentralized planning** and governance in rural areas, allowing local bodies to function as effective units of self-government.
 
• It enhanced the role of women and marginalized communities in governance by providing them with reserved seats in Panchayati Raj institutions.

questions.question: Which coastal plain is called the 'Hexadeltaic region' or 'Gift of six rivers'?

__
 
• **The coastal plain of Odisha** is called the "Hexadeltaic Region" or "The Gift of Six Rivers" It is called.
 
• This region is formed by **six major rivers** – Mahanadi, Brahmani, Baitarani, Subarnarekha, Rushikulya and Daya.
 
• This plain is located in the **Gulf region**, which is formed by sediments brought by rivers. This is known as the river delta.
 
• The coastal plain of Odisha provides **fertile land** and is suitable for agriculture. Rice, sugarcane, and other crops are produced here on a large scale.
 
• This region has **rich biodiversity** and is home to a wide variety of aquatic and terrestrial fauna.
 
• The coastal plain of Odisha is also an **important hub** for maritime trade and transportation.
 
• This region is home to important water bodies like **Chilka Lake**, which are important for tourism and ecology.
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Odisha's coastal plain.***

__
 
• **Coastal Plain of Odisha:**

 
 
• This plain is located in **Eastern India** and extends along the **Bay of Bengal**. Its average width is approximately **75-100 km**.
 
• The region is primarily composed of **deltaic** areas, formed by sediments carried by rivers.
 
• This plain is located **near sea level**, making it vulnerable to waterlogging and floods.
 
 
 
• **Six major rivers:**
 
 
• **Mahanadi:** It is the largest river in Odisha. It majorly influences the delta region of the plain.
 
• **Brahmani and Baitarani:** These rivers flow parallel and play an important role in the delta region.
 
• **Suvarnarekha:** It flows between West Bengal and Odisha.
 
• **Rushikulya and Daya:** These are smaller rivers but contribute to the formation of the delta.
 
 
 
• **Chilka Lake:**
 
 
• It is the largest brackish water lake in India and is located in the coastal plain of Odisha.
 
• This lake is an important habitat for aquatic life and birds.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Features of the Coastal Plain of Odisha:**

 
 
• This region provides **fertile land** and is important for agriculture.
 
• Floods and waterlogging are common here, affecting the ecology.
 
• It is important for **biodiversity** and environmental conservation.

questions.question: Who among the following was declared the leader of the rebellion by the rebels against British tyranny during the First War of Independence of 1857?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Bahadur Shah Zafar**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Bahadur Shah Zafar**, the last Mughal emperor, was declared the symbolic leader of the rebellion during the **First War of Independence of 1857**. His leadership was more symbolic as the rebels sought to unite under his name.
 
• The rebellion, also known as the **Sepoy Mutiny**, was a large-scale uprising against British colonial rule, triggered by various socio-economic, political, and religious grievances.
 
• Although Bahadur Shah Zafar was old and lacked the power to actively lead the rebellion, his position as the last Mughal emperor made him a unifying figure for the rebels. *Hence, he was declared the leader of the uprising.*
 
• The proclamation of Zafar as the leader symbolized the revolt against British imperialism and aimed to restore the Mughal Empire's glory. This was an attempt to rally Indian forces under a common identity.
 
• The British eventually captured Bahadur Shah Zafar, exiled him to Rangoon (present-day Yangon, Myanmar), and suppressed the rebellion, marking the end of the Mughal dynasty in India. *This marked a significant turning point in Indian history.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Other prominent leaders of the 1857 rebellion:**

 
 
• **Rani Laxmibai:** The Queen of Jhansi fought valiantly against the British forces and became a symbol of resistance during the rebellion.
 
• **Nana Saheb:** The adopted son of Peshwa Bajirao II led the rebellion in Kanpur and played a significant role in the revolt.
 
• **Shah Alam II:** Although not directly involved in the rebellion, he was a Mughal emperor whose rule preceded Zafar’s. He had no active role in 1857.
 
 
 
• **Key causes of the revolt:**
 
 
• **Social and religious grievances:** The imposition of British laws and policies like the abolition of Sati and introduction of Western education created discontent among Indians.
 
• **Economic exploitation:** Heavy taxation, land revenue policies, and the destruction of traditional industries led to widespread poverty.
 
• **Political reasons:** The Doctrine of Lapse and disrespect towards Indian rulers fueled dissatisfaction among the princely states.
 
 
 
• **Consequences of the rebellion:**
 
 
• The rebellion led to the dissolution of the East India Company, and the administration of India was transferred to the British Crown.
 
• The British government introduced reforms to appease Indians, including religious tolerance and protection of traditional practices.
 
• The revolt laid the foundation for the Indian freedom movement by fostering a sense of nationalism and unity among Indians.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **1857 rebellion significance:**

 
 
• The First War of Independence marked the first large-scale resistance against British colonial rule.
 
• It was both a military revolt and an expression of widespread discontent among civilians.
 
• The suppression of the rebellion led to reforms in British governance, including the end of Company rule and the establishment of direct Crown control.
 
 
 
• **Bahadur Shah Zafar’s legacy:**
 
 
• Despite his limited political role, Zafar is remembered for his symbolic significance in uniting Indians against British oppression.
 
• His exile marked the end of the Mughal Empire and remains a poignant reminder of colonial exploitation.

questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly describes India's foreign trade structure at the time of independence?

options.text: Export of raw materials and import of manufactured goods.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**कच्चे माल का निर्यात और निर्मित माल का आयात**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **At the time of India's independence (1947), the structure of foreign trade was highly imbalanced**. India was primarily an exporter of **raw materials** and an importer of **finished goods**. This was a direct consequence of colonial policies designed to serve British economic interests.
 
• India's exports mainly consisted of raw materials such as **cotton, jute, tea, and spices**. These were sent to Britain and other industrialized nations for processing and manufacturing.
 
• On the other hand, India imported a large quantity of finished goods, including **textiles, machinery, and other manufactured products**. This led to a dependency on foreign goods and suppressed domestic industries.
 
• The British colonial regime deliberately restricted the growth of Indian industries, ensuring that India remained a supplier of raw materials and a consumer of British goods. *Hence, this trade pattern was highly exploitative and one-sided.*
 
• The foreign trade during this period contributed to the **economic drain of wealth from India**, which was highlighted by Indian leaders such as **Dadabhai Naoroji** in his theory of economic drain. *Hence, statement 4 is correct.*
 
• Statements such as "Balanced trade" and "Complete trade isolation" are incorrect. India had an active trade relationship, but it was highly imbalanced and detrimental to India's economic interests.
 
• Statement "High export of finished goods" is also incorrect, as India primarily exported **raw materials**, not finished goods.
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is कच्चे माल का निर्यात और निर्मित माल का आयात.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Colonial Trade Policies:**

 
 
• The British implemented trade policies that prioritized their own economic interests. India was turned into a supplier of raw materials such as **cotton, indigo, jute, tea, and spices**, while British industries processed these materials and exported finished goods back to India.
 
• This trade structure suppressed the growth of Indian industries and caused significant economic hardships for Indian producers and laborers.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Foreign Trade on India's Economy:**
 
 
• The exploitative trade policies led to the **economic drain of wealth** from India, as highlighted by **Dadabhai Naoroji** in his book "Poverty and Un-British Rule in India."
 
• Indian artisans and small industries suffered greatly due to the import of cheap, mass-produced goods from Britain, which were sold at lower prices, driving local industries into decline.
 
• **Example:** The destruction of India's textile industry due to the import of British textiles is a significant historical instance of the adverse effects of colonial trade policies.
 
 
 
• **Post-Independence Trade Reforms:**
 
 
• After independence, India focused on developing domestic industries and reducing dependency on foreign goods. Policies were implemented to encourage industrial growth and self-reliance.
 
• The Indian government adopted import-substitution policies, focusing on producing goods domestically rather than importing them.
 
• For example, the establishment of public sector enterprises such as **Steel Authority of India (SAIL)** and **BHEL** aimed to strengthen India's industrial base.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key Features of India's Foreign Trade During Colonial Rule:**

 
 
• India was mainly an **exporter of raw materials** and an **importer of finished goods**.
 
• The colonial trade policies were designed to benefit Britain at India's expense, leading to the **economic exploitation** of India.
 
 
 
• **Relevance of Trade Structure Post-Independence:**
 
 
• India's focus shifted towards self-reliance, industrial development, and reducing dependency on foreign trade.
 
• Policies such as import substitution and industrialization aimed to rebuild India's economy and promote domestic manufacturing.
 
• **Example:** The Five-Year Plans emphasized industrial growth and the establishment of key industries such as steel, textiles, and engineering.

questions.question: In which of the following years did Sri Aurobindo resign from his post in Baroda and move to Calcutta and there he soon became a prominent leader of the nationalist movement?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1906**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Sri Aurobindo**, a prominent freedom fighter, philosopher, and spiritual leader, resigned from his post in Baroda in the year **1906**.
 
• After resigning, he moved to **Calcutta (now Kolkata)**, where he became actively involved in India's **nationalist movement**.
 
• Sri Aurobindo joined the **Indian National Congress** and emerged as one of the leading voices advocating for **complete independence**, rather than incremental reforms. *Hence, the statement about him moving to Calcutta in 1906 is correct.*
 
• His political writings and speeches inspired many Indians to join the struggle for freedom. He contributed significantly to revolutionary movements such as the **Swadeshi Movement** and the promotion of **boycotts against British goods.**
 
• Sri Aurobindo was instrumental in organizing secret groups for revolutionary activities. He also published articles in newspapers such as **Bande Mataram**, which became a platform for nationalist ideologies.
 
• Although he moved away from active politics in **1910** to settle in Pondicherry, his contributions during the early 20th century laid the foundation for India's independence movement. *Hence, the statement about his role in the nationalist movement in Calcutta is correct.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Sri Aurobindo's Early Life:**

 
 
• Sri Aurobindo was born on **15th August 1872** in Kolkata, India. He received education in England and later returned to India in **1893**.
 
• He joined the **Baroda State Service** in various administrative roles, including being a professor of English, and actively pursued literary and philosophical interests.
 
 
 
• **His Role in the Freedom Movement:**
 
 
• Sri Aurobindo played a significant role in the **Swadeshi Movement**, which encouraged Indians to boycott British goods and promote indigenous industries.
 
• He supported revolutionary activities and was linked to various secret societies like the **Anushilan Samiti**, which aimed to overthrow British rule.
 
• His writings in publications like **Bande Mataram** were instrumental in spreading nationalist ideas and inspiring the youth of India.
 
 
 
• **Transition to Spiritual Life:**
 
 
• In **1910**, Sri Aurobindo withdrew from active politics and moved to **Pondicherry**, where he focused on spiritual pursuits.
 
• He developed the philosophy of **Integral Yoga**, aiming to harmonize the spiritual and material aspects of life.
 
• His teachings and writings, including works like **The Life Divine** and **Savitri**, continue to inspire individuals worldwide.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Swadeshi Movement:**

 
 
• The **Swadeshi Movement** began in the early 20th century as a response to British colonial policies, particularly the partition of Bengal in **1905**.
 
• This movement encouraged Indians to boycott British goods and promote indigenous industries, including handloom weaving and crafts.
 
 
 
• **Bande Mataram Newspaper:**
 
 
• **Bande Mataram** was a nationalist publication started in **1905** to promote the Swadeshi Movement and revolutionary ideas.
 
• Sri Aurobindo was one of its primary contributors, using it as a platform to criticize British policies and inspire the masses.
 
 
 
• **Influence of Sri Aurobindo:**
 
 
• While Sri Aurobindo's active political career was brief, his contributions had a lasting impact on India's freedom struggle.
 
• His transition to spiritual life also influenced many leaders and thinkers, such as Mahatma Gandhi, who shared a vision of India's cultural and spiritual revival.

questions.question: Which of the following is a common feature of Dravidian temples?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gopuram**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Gopuram** is a monumental entrance tower that is a distinctive architectural feature of **Dravidian temples**. It acts as the gateway to the temple complex.
 
• The **Gopuram** is typically adorned with intricate sculptures depicting **Hindu deities, mythological stories, and decorative motifs**.
 
• It is located at the entrance of the temple and serves as an identifying landmark of Dravidian temple architecture. *Hence, this feature is correct.*
 
• **Dravidian temples** are known for their pyramidal structure, and the Gopuram dominates the skyline, acting as the **visual focal point** of the temple complex.
 
• The construction of Gopurams gained prominence during the **Chola, Pandya, and Vijayanagara dynasties**, showcasing elaborate designs. *Hence, this is a defining feature of Dravidian temples.*
 
• Other options like **Pillarless Hall**, **Sikhara**, and **Flat Roof** do not align with the architectural characteristics of Dravidian temples.
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Gopuram.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Dravidian Temple Architecture:**

 
 
• **Dravidian architecture** emerged in South India and is characterized by its **towering Gopurams, enclosed courtyards, and intricate carvings**.
 
• These temples were constructed using granite and sandstone, showcasing **engineering brilliance** during the Chola and Vijayanagara periods.
 
 
 
• **Gopuram Features:**
 
 
• Gopurams are constructed in a **pyramidal shape** with multiple tiers and are often decorated with sculptures representing **Hindu mythology**.
 
• The **Vijayanagara dynasty** contributed significantly to the development of massive Gopurams, such as the Gopuram of the **Meenakshi Temple** in Madurai.
 
 
 
• **Historical Examples:**
 
 
• **Brihadeeswarar Temple** (Tamil Nadu): Built during the Chola Dynasty, the temple features a prominent Gopuram.
 
• **Meenakshi Amman Temple** (Madurai): Famous for its towering Gopurams and detailed sculptures.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Pillarless Hall:**

 
 
• Dravidian temples generally have halls supported by intricately carved pillars, not pillarless halls. This feature is not common in South Indian temples.
 
 
 
• **Sikhara:**
 
 
• The Sikhara, or spire, is more commonly associated with **Nagara-style temples** of North India, not Dravidian temples.
 
 
 
• **Flat Roof:**
 
 
• Dravidian temples have pyramidal roofs rather than flat roofs, which is a defining feature of their architecture.

questions.question: Which of the following Indian states has the highest elevation point in India (excluding POK)?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sikkim**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Kanchenjunga**, located in the state of **Sikkim**, is the highest elevation point in India (excluding Pakistan-occupied Kashmir). It stands at a towering height of **8,586 meters**, making it the third-highest mountain in the world.
 
• This peak is part of the **Himalayan mountain range** and lies on the border of India and Nepal. The majority of Kanchenjunga's massif lies within Sikkim, India.
 
• Sikkim's unique geographical location, surrounded by the Eastern Himalayas, contributes to the presence of such high-altitude peaks. *Hence, Sikkim is the correct answer.*
 
• Other states like **Himachal Pradesh**, **Uttarakhand**, and **Arunachal Pradesh** also host high-altitude peaks, but none of them surpass Kanchenjunga in terms of elevation.
 
• In Himachal Pradesh, the highest peak is **Reo Purgyil** at an elevation of **6,816 meters**, while in Uttarakhand, **Nanda Devi** stands at **7,816 meters**, and Arunachal Pradesh features **Kangto** at **7,042 meters**.
 
• Despite these impressive peaks, **Sikkim's Kanchenjunga** remains the highest elevation point in India (excluding POK) and is internationally recognized as a key landmark of the country. *Hence, the other options are incorrect.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Kanchenjunga:**

 
 
• **Kanchenjunga** is sacred to the people of Sikkim and is considered the guardian deity of the state. Climbing the peak is restricted due to its cultural and spiritual significance.
 
• It is a part of the **Greater Himalayas** and is renowned for its biodiversity, hosting rare species like the **red panda** and **snow leopard**.
 
• Kanchenjunga’s name means “The Five Treasures of Snows,” referring to its five distinct peaks, which symbolize the treasures of gold, silver, gems, grain, and sacred texts.
 
 
 
• **Other High Peaks in India:**

questions.question: What is the most common cause of a tsunami?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Subsea earthquake**__.

• **Tsunamis are primarily caused by Subsea Earthquakes:** A **subsea earthquake** occurs when tectonic plates beneath the ocean move abruptly, displacing large volumes of water. This sudden displacement generates powerful waves, leading to tsunamis.
 
• The energy released during the earthquake transfers to the water above, creating high-energy waves that can travel thousands of kilometers across the ocean.
 
• The most common type of earthquake causing a tsunami is a **megathrust earthquake**. These occur at convergent plate boundaries where one tectonic plate is forced beneath another. *Hence, subsea earthquakes are the primary cause of tsunamis.*
 
• **Other causes:** While subsea earthquakes are the most common cause, tsunamis can also be triggered by volcanic eruptions, underwater landslides, or asteroid impacts. However, these are relatively rare compared to earthquakes.
 
• Heavy rainfall, flooding, cyclones, and high tides do not cause tsunamis directly. These are unrelated phenomena. *Hence, options 1, 3, and 4 are incorrect.*
 
• **Impact of tsunamis:** Tsunamis often result in massive destruction along coastlines, including loss of life, property damage, and environmental degradation. Coastal areas are especially vulnerable.
 
• The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, triggered by a megathrust earthquake off the coast of Sumatra, is one of the deadliest examples. It caused significant damage in several countries, including India, Sri Lanka, and Indonesia. *Hence, subsea earthquakes are correctly identified as the primary cause.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Characteristics of Subsea Earthquakes:**

 
 
• **Location:** These occur at tectonic plate boundaries, particularly at subduction zones where plates collide.
 
• **Energy release:** Subsea earthquakes release massive energy, displacing water and triggering waves. The stronger the earthquake, the higher the energy released.
 
• **Magnitude:** Earthquakes with a magnitude of 7.0 or higher are more likely to generate tsunamis.
 
 
 
• **Examples of tsunamis caused by subsea earthquakes:**
 
 
• **2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami:** A megathrust earthquake of magnitude 9.1 off the coast of Sumatra triggered this tsunami, which caused over 230,000 deaths.
 
• **2011 Japan Tsunami:** A magnitude 9.0 earthquake off the coast of Tohoku led to massive destruction, including the Fukushima nuclear disaster.
 
 
 
• **Other causes of tsunamis:**
 
 
• **Volcanic eruptions:** Explosive underwater eruptions can displace water and create tsunamis. Example: Krakatoa eruption in 1883.
 
• **Underwater landslides:** Landslides triggered by earthquakes can displace water, generating waves.
 
• **Asteroid impacts:** Although rare, large asteroids striking oceans can produce tsunamis. Example: Chicxulub impact that contributed to dinosaur extinction.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key facts about tsunamis:**

 
 
• **Speed:** Tsunami waves can travel at speeds of up to 800 km/h in deep water.
 
• **Wave height:** While tsunamis are barely noticeable in deep oceans, their height increases dramatically as they approach shallow coastal areas.
 
• **Warning systems:** Advanced tsunami warning systems, like those established in the Pacific Ocean, help reduce casualties by providing early alerts.
 
 
 
• **Global efforts to mitigate tsunami impacts:**

questions.question: Before its repeal in 2019, which of the following was the key feature of Article 370 that gave special status to Jammu and Kashmir?

options.text: Parliament required the consent of the state government to make laws on matters in the Union List for Jammu and Kashmir.
The provisions of the Directive Principles of State Policy were fully applicable in the state.
Jammu and Kashmir had no representation in the Lok Sabha.
Jammu and Kashmir could not be included in the First Schedule of the Constitution.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Parliament required the consent of the state government to make laws on matters in the Union List for Jammu and Kashmir**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 370** of the **Indian Constitution** provided special autonomy to **Jammu and Kashmir**. It allowed the state to have its own Constitution and limited the Indian Parliament's legislative powers over the state.
 
• Under **Article 370**, **Parliament required the consent of the state government** to legislate on matters specified in the **Union List** and **Concurrent List**. This was a significant departure from the powers Parliament has over other states in India. *Hence, this statement is correct.*
 
• The provisions of the **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)** were not fully applicable to Jammu and Kashmir due to its special status. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.*
 
• **Jammu and Kashmir** had representation in the Lok Sabha, just like other states. It sent representatives to the Indian Parliament, disproving the claim that it lacked representation. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.*
 
• Jammu and Kashmir was included in the **First Schedule** of the Constitution, which lists the states and union territories of India. It was never excluded from this schedule. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.*
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is Parliament required the consent of the state government to make laws on matters in the Union List for Jammu and Kashmir.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Article 370: Special Status of Jammu and Kashmir:**

 
 
• **Article 370** was part of the Constitution that granted special autonomy to Jammu and Kashmir. This provision was introduced because the state had its own **Constitution**, adopted in 1956.
 
• Under Article 370, the **Indian Parliament** could legislate for Jammu and Kashmir only on defense, foreign affairs, and communication, unless the state government consented to extend other Union laws.
 
 
 
• **Key Features of Article 370:**
 
 
• Jammu and Kashmir had its own **Constitution**, separate from the Indian Constitution.
 
• Indian laws were not automatically applicable in Jammu and Kashmir, unlike other states.
 
• The citizens of Jammu and Kashmir were governed by **state-specific laws**, including laws related to property ownership and citizenship.
 
 
 
• **Repeal of Article 370:**
 
 
• On **August 5, 2019**, the Indian government abrogated Article 370, revoking Jammu and Kashmir's special status.
 
• This decision led to the bifurcation of the state into two **Union Territories**: Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Impact of Article 370:**

 
 
• It created a unique relationship between Jammu and Kashmir and the Indian Union, where the state enjoyed greater autonomy than other states.
 
• The abrogation of Article 370 sparked debates on its constitutional and political implications, with supporters arguing it would lead to better integration of the state with India and critics expressing concerns over federalism and regional sentiments.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context:**
 
 
• Article 370 was introduced following the **Instrument of Accession** signed by Maharaja Hari Singh in **1947**, when Jammu and Kashmir joined India.
 
• Over the years, several provisions of the Indian Constitution were extended to Jammu and Kashmir, gradually eroding its special status before the final repeal in **2019**.
